case.title: The House That Stood
case.hook: It’s June. Storm Night is over, and the Rivera family has to rebuild their house on Bay Street. Remember the Mexico Beach photos? A few houses were still standing. The Riveras asked me: how do we build a house that stands up to the next storm? Let’s find out, then design one.

notice.head: Building permit · Palmetto Springs
notice.title: Rebuild the Rivera house, 214 Bay Street
rows: On Storm Night, seawater filled the house 4 feet deep. The family had evacuated and was safe.
A new house on Bay Street must keep its floor above the storm-surge line.
7 coins for storm protection (pretend money for this lesson).
notice.line: The town signs the permit when the plan passes the storm tests.

stills.alt: Two beach houses still standing after Hurricane Michael. A window is covered with wood boards, a blue tarp covers part of a roof, and the deck and steps below are broken.

case.stillsCredit: Damaged houses after Hurricane Michael, Mexico Beach, Florida, 14 October 2018: Voice of America (VOA), via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). The Riveras, Palmetto Springs and the permit are made up for this lesson.
case.question: How should the Riveras rebuild so their house stands up to the next storm?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: The storm hit hardest near the ground: waves broke the deck and steps. Boards kept a window safe, but wind tore up part of a roof.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: three kinds of mitigation
clues.t: There are three kinds of mitigation: built (shutters, roof straps), natural (mangroves, dunes) and planning (evacuation routes, storm plans).

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: build it, then storm it
clues.t: The house stood when its floor was on deep pilings above the surge, its roof was strapped down and its windows were covered, all inside the budget.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: fix the whole town
clues.t: One fix can’t solve every problem. Palmetto Springs needs a mix of built, natural and planning fixes.

solve.title: How should the Riveras rebuild?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Build the same house again, just bigger.
options.why: Check Clue 1. Where did the storm do the most damage?

options.t: Build a tall wall around the house. That’s all it needs.
options.why: Check Clue 3. What did the house need to pass every test?

options.t: Raise it on deep pilings above the surge, strap the roof down, cover the windows, stay inside the budget, and test the plan first. One fix isn’t enough.
options.why: Case cracked! You combined several kinds of mitigation and tested your design, just like real engineers. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

photos.afterText: look at what a real storm did to real houses
photos.kicker: Warm-Up game · a real Florida street
photos.title: What helped? What failed?
todo: Tap each number on the photo and read what happened there.
Then match each clue to a number.

why.t: Mexico Beach, Florida, four days after Hurricane Michael. These houses are still standing, but the storm hit them hard.

photos.alt: Two beach houses still standing after Hurricane Michael. A window is covered with wood boards, a blue tarp covers part of a roof, and the deck and steps below are broken.
photos.credit: Damaged houses after Hurricane Michael, Mexico Beach, Florida, 14 October 2018: Voice of America (VOA), via Wikimedia Commons

hotspots.label: Boards on the window
hotspots.t: Before the storm, someone covered this window with plywood boards. Boards stop flying branches and trash from breaking the glass. The window made it.

hotspots.label: Blue tarp on the roof
hotspots.t: The wind tore up part of this roof. A blue tarp keeps the rain out until it can be fixed. This roof needed a stronger tie-down.

hotspots.label: The fallen deck
hotspots.t: The deck under the house fell down. Waves and storm surge hit hardest close to the ground.

hotspots.label: Broken steps
hotspots.t: Waves broke these concrete steps and blocks apart and pushed them around.

task.q: Match each clue to a number on the photo.
task.win: The storm hit hardest near the ground, and wind went after the roof. That’s a clue.

items.evid: Plywood boards kept a window from breaking.
The wind tore up part of a roof.

items.step: Damage from waves near the ground
items.evid: Waves broke the deck and steps near the ground.

mitsort.afterText: Florida towns use a mix of three kinds
mitsort.title: Three kinds of mitigation
todo: Drag each card onto its shelf (or tap a card, then a shelf).

shelves.sub: living things and land that slow storms

cards.alt: Dark wooden shutters closed over two tall windows of a yellow house.
cards.why: People hang shutters so flying trash can’t break the windows.
cards.miss: Shutters are made and put up by people. Which shelf is for things people build?

cards.alt: A builder hammers nails into the wooden frame of a new house’s roof.
cards.t: Metal hurricane straps that tie the roof to the walls
cards.why: Florida’s building code says new houses need roof ties like these, so wind can’t lift the roof off.
cards.miss: Builders nail these into the house. Which shelf is that?

cards.alt: Mangrove trees with tangled roots growing along calm water.
cards.why: Tangled mangrove roots slow down waves before they reach land.
cards.miss: Mangroves are living trees. Which shelf is for living things?

cards.alt: Sea oats growing on a sandy dune.
cards.t: Sand dunes held by sea oats
cards.why: Waves hit the dune first. Sea oat roots hold the sand in place.
cards.miss: Dunes and sea oats are land and plants. Which shelf is that?

cards.alt: A blue Evacuation Route sign with an arrow, next to palm trees.
cards.why: Signs show the safest roads away from the coast. A plan keeps people safe even when buildings can’t.
cards.miss: The sign is part of a plan that tells people where to go. Which shelf is that?

cards.t: A family storm plan: where to go, what to pack, who to call
cards.why: A plan made before storm season helps a family leave quickly and safely.
cards.miss: This is something a family decides ahead of time. Which shelf is that?

mitsort.doneLine: Every card is on a shelf.
mitsort.q: Why do Florida towns use all three kinds?

opts.t: Each kind protects in a different way, so together they cover more.
One kind always works best, so towns try to find it.
opts.miss: If one kind always worked best, would towns bother with the others?

opts.t: Natural mitigation is free, so it doesn’t count.
opts.miss: Planting and caring for dunes and mangroves takes work and money, too.

mitsort.credit: Storm shutters, Vero Beach, 2004: Mark Wolfe, FEMA (public domain). Hurricane straps at a Habitat for Humanity home, Pensacola, 2008: U.S. Navy photo by Gary Nichols (public domain). Mangrove shoreline, Biscayne National Park: National Park Service (public domain). Sea oats on a sand dune, John U. Lloyd Beach State Park: Georgialh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Evacuation route sign near Boca Raton: Juliancolton (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.
mitsort.win: Built, natural and planning: three kinds of mitigation. That’s a clue.

buildhouse.afterText: then compare at least two possible solutions
buildhouse.title: Build it, then storm it
todo: Pick a foundation, windows and a roof for the Riveras’ house. Each ● costs a coin.
Press Run the storm. If a test fails, change one part and run it again.

why.t: In Mexico Beach, the “Sand Palace” sat on 40-foot pilings, with its first floor 15 feet up, strong concrete walls and few windows. It stood while most houses around it were destroyed.

opts.note: The floor sits right on the ground. It’s cheap, but any flood water comes right in.
Better, but the storm surge here reaches 8 feet.
Long poles driven deep into the ground lift the floor above the surge. Water flows underneath.
Flying branches can break plain glass. Then wind and rain rush in.
Shutters close over the glass before a storm.
Extra-strong glass that doesn’t shatter. Nothing to close before a storm, but it costs more.
The roof is held on only by nails.
Metal straps tie the roof to the walls so wind can’t lift it.

tests.pass: The floor is 10 feet up. The surge flowed under the house.
tests.fail: Seawater came inside. The floor is below the 8-foot surge line.
A flying branch broke the glass. Wind and rain blew inside.

tests.t: Roof stays on in 130 mph wind
tests.pass: The straps held the roof down.
tests.fail: The wind lifted the roof off. It was only nailed down.

buildhouse.startLine: Pick each part, then run the storm.
buildhouse.overLine: Over budget! That breaks the constraint (the limit). Can a cheaper part still pass its test?
buildhouse.reviseLine: Look at the red ❌ tests. Change one part at a time, then run the storm again.
buildhouse.passLine: Every test passed, and it fits the budget. The town can sign the permit.
buildhouse.deepLabel: pilings go deep into the ground
buildhouse.q: Why didn’t impact glass make it into the final design?

opts.t: It costs too much for the budget, and shutters passed the same test.

opts.miss: Look at its note: impact glass doesn’t shatter. What was the problem?

opts.t: Windows don’t matter in a storm.
opts.miss: What happened to the plain glass in the test?

buildhouse.win: Raise it, strap it, cover it, and stay in budget. That’s a clue.

fixtown.afterText: Open each problem on the map
fixtown.title: Fix the whole town
todo: Tap a problem on the list or a pin on the map.
Pick the fix that would help most. Then stamp it: built, natural or planning.
fixtown.kindQ: What kind of mitigation is it?

spots.problem: A big branch snapped and blocked the road.

fixes.t: Plant wind-resistant trees, like live oaks, away from the road
Cut down every tree in town
fixes.miss: That would lose shade and homes for birds. Is there a smarter way?
People need the road. What could keep it clear?

kindMiss.built: Trees aren’t built by people. They’re living things.
kindMiss.plan: Planting is an action, but the fix itself is a living thing. Which kind is that?

spots.why: Some trees, like live oaks, hold up better in strong wind. Planting them away from roads keeps falling branches out of the way.

spots.problem: A power line came down, and the power went out.

fixes.t: Turn off the power every summer
fixes.miss: Families need power all summer. What could protect the lines?

fixes.t: Paint the poles a brighter color
fixes.miss: Paint won’t stop wind. What would keep the lines away from the wind?

kindMiss.natural: Power lines and pipes are made by people. Which kind is that?
kindMiss.plan: Workers dig and lay new lines. Is that a plan or something built?

spots.why: Lines under the ground can’t be blown down by wind or hit by falling trees.

spots.problem: The street flooded when the storm drains overflowed.

fixes.t: Add rain gardens: low gardens with plants that soak up rainwater
Pave the yards so water runs off faster
fixes.miss: Pavement sends MORE water into the street. What would soak it up?

fixes.t: Ask people to stay inside when it rains
fixes.miss: The street would still flood. What could hold the water?

kindMiss.built: A rain garden is made of soil and plants. Which kind is that?
kindMiss.plan: A rain garden is plants and soil, not a plan. Which kind is that?

spots.why: Plants and loose soil soak up rain like a sponge, so less water rushes into the drains at once.

fixes.t: Rebuild the houses on deep pilings, like the Riveras’
Paint the houses with waterproof paint
fixes.miss: Paint won’t keep 8 feet of water out. What would lift the house above it?
The bay can’t move! What can change about the houses?

kindMiss.natural: Pilings are made by people. Which kind is that?
kindMiss.plan: Pilings are part of the building. Which kind is that?

spots.why: Raised floors let the surge flow under the house, like the Riveras’ design in Part 2.

spots.problem: Some families waited too long to leave.

fixes.t: Practice the evacuation plan every June and post route signs
Wait until the water arrives, then decide
fixes.miss: By then the roads may be flooded. When should families decide?
A building doesn’t tell people when and where to go. What would?

kindMiss.built: Practice and signs tell people what to do. Is that built, or a plan?
kindMiss.natural: Practice isn’t a living thing. Which kind is it?

spots.why: Families who practice know when to leave and which road to take, so they get out before the storm arrives.

fixtown.q: What makes the best plan for Palmetto Springs?

opts.t: A mix of built, natural and planning fixes, one for each problem.
One giant seawall around the whole town.
opts.miss: Would a wall stop a falling branch or a flooded Elm Street?

opts.t: Only planning, because buildings always fail.
opts.miss: The Riveras’ house passed every test. Do buildings always fail?

fixtown.win: Each problem needed its own fix. Together they make a plan. That’s your last clue.

q1.A: You can’t stop a hurricane. What CAN engineers change?
q1.B: Forecasters predict storms. What does mitigation do?

q2.A: Built means people make it out of concrete or wood. Are mangroves built?
q2.C: A plan is something people agree to follow. Are mangroves a plan?

q3.B: A criterion is a goal. Is the berm a goal, or a change to the design?
q3.C: A constraint is a limit, like a budget. Is the berm a limit?

cer-4.label: your reasoning
cer-4.re: because|so |this shows|that shows|this means|that means|which means|proves|since

ans-2: Think about the three shelves. What does a built solution do well? A natural one?
What could a seawall do that mangroves can’t, and the other way around?
Try: It is useful to compare them because ___. For example, ___.
ans-3: What happened when one of your house tests failed?
Think of two fixes that cover each other’s weak spots, like shutters AND roof straps.
Try: Revision is important because ___. For example, a town could combine ___ and ___.
cer-4: First decide: is a tall wall the ONLY way to protect a town?
Think about the Riveras’ house and the problems on the town map.
Try: I ___ because ___. One piece of evidence is ___. Another is ___.

planner.title: Your claim and two pieces of evidence

rows.label: 2. Pick two pieces of evidence from the lesson
options: The Riveras’ house stood because of pilings, roof straps and shutters, not a wall.
A wall can’t stop a falling branch, a downed power line or rain flooding Elm Street.
Mangroves and dunes are natural mitigation that slow waves before they reach land.
Evacuation plans keep people safe even when buildings get damaged.

planner.note: Tap your side and two facts. Then write your reasoning in your own words.

welcome.label: Welcome · the house that stood
welcome.script: Hi, it’s June. Storm Night is over, and the Rivera family needs to rebuild their house on Bay Street. Remember those Mexico Beach photos? A few houses were still standing. The Riveras asked me a big question: how do we build a house that stands up to the next storm? Let’s find out together, then design one.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · what helped, what failed? (Clue 1)
warmup.script: This is a real street in Mexico Beach, four days after the storm. Tap each number on the photo and read what happened there. Then match the clues. Look closely: where did the storm do the most damage?

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Hold up a cardboard “budget” of 7 coins for “constraint”; act out “revise” by fixing a paper house and trying again.

part1.label: Part 1 · three kinds of mitigation (Clue 2)
part1.script: Engineers have three kinds of tools for a storm: things we build, natural helpers like dunes and mangroves, and plans people follow. Drag each photo onto the right shelf. Which kind do you think Florida towns use most?

part2.label: Part 2 · build it, then storm it (Clue 3)
part2.script: Time to design the Riveras’ house. Pick a foundation, windows and a roof, but watch the budget. Then run the storm. If a test fails, don’t worry. Change one part and try again. That’s what engineers do.

explore.label: Part 4 · fix the whole town (Clue 4)
explore.script: The Riveras have their plan. Now the town council wants one for the whole town. Tap each problem from Storm Night on the map. Pick the fix that would help most, then decide: is it built, natural or a plan?

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: how should the Riveras rebuild? Then answer two questions, plan a fix for any Florida hazard in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

partc.label: Part C · design a mitigation plan

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says the only way to protect a town is the tallest, strongest wall you can build. Hmm. Think about the Riveras’ house, and think about Elm Street. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease the review days (17.R1: a mystery on Main Street).
closing.script: Case closed! You studied a real storm, built a house that passed every test, and made a plan for the whole town. That’s what engineers do: they can’t stop a hurricane, but they can lower the harm. Next time, it’s review time. Get ready for a mystery on Main Street.

camera.huntTitle: Bonus: can you snap all 4 shots on this list?
missions: The photo with all four numbers opened (Warm-Up)
Your house passing the storm test (The Lesson)
The town map with every problem fixed (The Lesson)

sketch.tip: Draw with the pen. Then use 🏷️ Label: drag from a part of your sketch to an empty spot, and type its name.
prompts: My fix for one Florida hazard
Draw a small table: solutions across the top, criteria down the side
Circle the winner and write your revision

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how people design ways to lower the harm of a natural hazard?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Deep pilings lift the floor above the storm surge.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “pilings”, “floor above” and “surge”. Those words tell how the design beats the hazard. Small words like “the” don’t carry the idea.
